title: 全国的に大気不安定 急な雷雨注意
body:
今日30日は全国的に大気の状態が不安定になり、局地的には激しい雨が降るでしょう。晴れ間の出る所も、急な雨や雷雨に注意が必要です。関東から北海道は昨日29日より気温が高く、寒さが和らぐでしょう。
今日30日は、上空に流れ込む寒気や湿った空気の影響で、全国的に大気の状態が不安定になるでしょう。落雷や竜巻などの激しい突風、急に強まる雨にご注意ください。九州や四国、中国地方は昼頃まで雨が降り、近畿や東海、北陸は断続的に雨が降るでしょう。局地的には雷を伴って雨脚が強まり、激しい雨が降ることもありそうです。関東甲信は雲が広がりやすく、所々で雨が降るでしょう。東北は日本海側を中心に雨が降り、雷を伴う所もありそうです。北海道は晴れ間が出ますが、日本海側を中心に所々で雨や雷雨となるでしょう。雪が積もっている所では、路面状況の悪化にご注意ください。沖縄も、所々でにわか雨がありそうです。
最高気温は、昨日29日と同じくらいか高い所が多いでしょう。九州と四国は25℃以上の夏日になる所があり、中国地方は23℃前後の所が多くなりそうです。昼間は薄着で過ごせるくらいでしょう。近畿と東海は昨日より低く、昼間もヒンヤリと感じられそうです。北陸は20℃に届かない所が多くい、一日を通して上着が必要になるでしょう。関東や東北、北海道は南よりの風が強まって、昨日より5℃以上高い所もありそうです。平年より高い所もあり、東京都心は22℃と昼前後は長袖シャツ一枚で過ごせるくらいでしょう。朝晩は羽織るもので調節してください。

title: 富士山の初冠雪を確認 気象庁発表
body: 気象庁は10月30日、富士山の初冠雪が確認されたと発表しました。富士山の初冠雪は、1894年の統計開始以来、甲府地方気象台により「目視」で観測されてきましたが、気象庁は、今季から、アメダスや雨雲レーダー、衛星画像をもとに、山頂付近の積雪をデータで「解析」し、自動で判定する形に切り替わりました。【写真を見る】初冠雪した富士山=静岡県富士市・田子の浦港、10月30日朝方法が変わったため単純比較はできませんが、目視による富士山の初冠雪の平年日は10月2日で、2025年は10月23日に観測されていました。

title: 株価崩れない「ホンダ」の強み
body:
※あのニュースはどんな業界に影響するのか、あの企業の株価が動いたのはなぜか……。連載「ニュースで読み解く！注目株」では、株式市場を知り尽くした執筆陣が、いま注目すべき銘柄や相場の展開を解説します。日経平均株価が下落するなかでも上昇した本田技研工業の株価チャート日経平均株価が調整局面に入るなか、自動車大手の本田技研工業＜7267＞（以下、ホンダ）の株価が底堅さを保っています。相場が大きく崩れた10月中旬にも上昇を続け、21日には年初来高値を付けました。上場来高値にも近づいています。自動車業界では、電気自動車（EV）を巡る競争や中東情勢など不透明な材料も少なくありません。一方で、ホンダにとっては好材料となる要素も複数観測されています。根強いハイブリッド車人気と四輪車以外の好調さ、フィジカルAIへの期待です。
EVへの関心が世界的に高まる一方、実際のクルマ選びでは、購入価格や使い勝手を重視する消費者も少なくありません。そうしたなかで、アメリカでは利益率の高いハイブリッド車（HV）が改めて支持を集めています。理由のひとつは、ガソリン車に近い感覚で乗れることです。EVは自宅や外出先での充電が必要ですが、HVなら給油するだけで走り続けられます。充電設備の普及状況を気にする必要がなく、長距離の移動でも使いやすいのが特徴です。もちろん、燃費の良さも大きな魅力です。ガソリン価格が高くなれば、燃料代を抑えられるHVの利点は一段と際立ちます。EVへの全面的な切り替えには踏み切れないものの、燃費は改善したい。そんな消費者にとって、HVは現実的な選択肢になっています。この流れは、ホンダにとって大きな商機です。同社は長年培ってきたエンジン技術に電動化技術を組み合わせ、HVの商品力を高めてきました。EVの普及を急ぐだけでなく、実際の需要が伸びている分野に力を入れることで、販売台数の拡大を狙っています。ホンダは2027年以降、次世代ハイブリッドシステムを搭載した新型車を投入する計画です。2030年3月期までに世界で15車種を展開する方針も掲げています。アメリカでHVを選ぶ消費者が増えるなか、商品ラインアップの充実が販売増につながるかが注目されます。

title: 市が高級ピアノ買い替え決定 賛否
body:
世界三大ピアノのひとつ『スタインウェイ』。鎌倉市が所有するこのピアノが、約4400万円で買い替えられるといいます。33年間愛された名器の買い替えは“芸術への投資”か、それとも“税金の無駄遣い”か…市民からは賛否の声が上がっています。【ニュースto】富山市が人口を“2000人以上”水増し！“組織的”として市長が謝罪　誰が何のために？
神奈川県鎌倉市にある鎌倉芸術館。ここに、33年にわたり音色を響かせてきたグランドピアノがあります｡世界三大ピアノのひとつと称される『スタインウェイ』。特徴は、なんといってもその音色です｡170年以上にわたり受け継がれてきた、熟練の職人たちの技と、手作業から生まれる華やかな響きで、世界中の演奏家を魅了してきた名器です。鎌倉芸術館が所有するグランドピアノは、合わせて4台で、アメリカの『スタインウェイ』のほか、オーストリアの『ベーゼンドルファー』、国産の『ヤマハ』と『カワイ』があります。その中で演奏家が求める繊細な表現にも応えてきた、『スタインウェイ』のピアノですが、33年という歳月は、ある深刻な変化をもたらしていました｡
(スタインウェイ社の説明)｢全体的な音量の低下や細やかな雑音の発生等、楽器としての性能の低下がみられます。修理に必要な純正パーツの供給がないことに加え、修理を行ったとしても、十分な性能回復は見込めません｣メーカー側から、長年の使用による劣化に加え、修理にも限界があると指摘されたのです。さらに演奏家など、利用者からも“自身の演奏の表現ができない”、“以前より音色が異なってきている”といった趣旨の意見が寄せられたといいます。アーティストが求める音を、これまで通り届けられないとして、鎌倉市は買い替えを決断しました。その購入金額は約4400万円です。国内外の著名な演奏家を招致し、質の高い音楽を届けるためにも重要だという『スタインウェイ』のピアノですが…。

title: エスカレーターを歩く人 傾向分析
body:
エスカレーターの片側に立ち止まり、もう片側を歩く――。歩かずに乗るよう呼びかけられているものの、実際にはこんな光景を見ることが多いのではないでしょうか。エスカレーターでの歩行を調査した研究者に、どんな人がどんなケースで歩いているのか聞きました。（朝日新聞withnews編集部・河原夏季）【動画】AIが、歩く人に注意する様子
エスカレーターを歩いている人について研究したのは、岩手県立大学名誉教授の元田良孝さん（交通工学）です。元田さんによると、エスカレーターを歩く人が特に多い場所は駅だといいます。元田さんたちが2019年に東京メトロの国会議事堂前・後楽園・赤坂見附の3駅で実施した調査（n＝11017）では、歩く人の割合は37.3％でした。鉄道会社や業界団体は立ち止まって乗るように再三呼びかけていますが、どうして歩く人が後を絶たないのでしょうか。元田さんは「理由は非常に単純な話で、早く移動したい人がいるからです」と話します。「歩きたいのではなく、電車の時間に間に合わないといった理由が十分に考えられます」
立ち止まるか、歩くかの選択には、エスカレーターの上り下りや交通量、乗っているときの動作なども関係していることが、元田さんたちの調査でわかりました。エスカレーターの上りと下りの歩行率を比較すると、上りの平均は26.3％だった一方、下りは48.4％でした。元田さんは「下りは進行方向に重力で引っ張られるので歩きやすく、上るほうが労力がかかる」と分析します。しかし、利用者が多くなると立ち止まって乗る側に行列ができるので、上り下りにかかわらず、並ぶことを避けるために歩く人がいるそうです。朝と夕方の通勤時間帯には歩行率が高くなるといいます。
このほか、スマートフォンの操作や電話といった「ながら動作」をする人は、歩く割合が低かったそうです。また、年齢が高いと歩く人が少ないこともわかりました。調査した3駅の混雑時の平均では、60歳以上と思われる人が19.7％、60歳未満と思われる人は40.8％でした。性別でみると、男性41.9％に対し、女性は36.1％でした。しかし、上りでは男性のほうが歩いていた一方、下りでは性別による差は見られなかったといいます。元田さんは「年齢も男女の差も、身体能力の違いが表れていると考えられます」と話します。

title: NVIDIAトップに中国工作員接近か
body: 米紙ニューヨーク・タイムズ（NYT）は29日、中国情報機関の工作員が半導体大手エヌビディアのジェンスン・フアン最高経営責任者（CEO）と親密な関係を築き、中国に製品に関する情報を流していた可能性があると報じた。約1年前にトランプ大統領にも報告されたが、何の対応も取られなかったとしている。【英MI5が警告】中国からの研究資金、狙いは「スパイに役立つ知識」NYTは、米情報機関から説明を受けた匿名の情報筋の話として報じた。工作員はシンガポールに拠点を置くデータセンター幹部の女性で、同データセンターがエヌビディア製の高性能AIチップを中国に不正に横流しした疑いに対する捜査のなかで浮上したという。フアン氏はトランプ氏と親しく、今年5月の訪中にも随行した。トランプ氏が対応を取らなかったことについて、エヌビディアの取引に影響を及ぼすことや、中国との貿易関係を複雑化させることを懸念したという見方をNYTは報じている。また、NYTは「トランプ氏とフアン氏の親密な関係が、エヌビディア製チップの海外向け販売の取り締まりを阻害している」という米当局者の話も伝えた。米商務省内では、中国やエヌビディアに関係する貿易への調査や制裁案が、一部滞っているという。（鈴木峻）

title: スペインの列車事故 死者69人に
body: 【パリ時事】スペイン中部トレド県で28日に高速列車同士が衝突した事故で、同国メディアは29日、死者が69人になったと伝えた。【ひと目でわかる】スペイン列車事故現場重軽傷者は180～200人に上る。現場では救助・捜索活動が続いた。木原稔官房長官は29日の記者会見で、乗客名簿に日本人2人の氏名が載っていたとの連絡をスペイン当局から受けたと明らかにした。在スペイン日本大使館に現地対策本部を設置し、2人の安否確認を急いでいる。サンチェス首相は28日、同県ウルダの事故現場を視察。29日から3日間を服喪期間にすると述べ、「高速鉄道の信頼回復と利用者の安全確保に向け、必要な措置を断固として講じる」と訴えた。衝突した2本の列車には計約540人が乗車していた。運行の自動管理システムに不具合が生じ、先行する列車が停止。その後、管制センターが手動に切り替え後続列車に進行を許可し、惨事につながった。プエンテ運輸相は記者団に、管制の判断について「説明がつかない」と批判した。ブラジルから観光でスペインを訪れ、列車に乗り合わせた女性は公共放送に「（座席で）眠っていて、目覚めたら体が宙を舞っていた」と衝撃の大きさを語った。一方、男性乗客は「ハイテク技術がそろっているのに、衝突は理解できない」と怒りをあらわにした。スペインでは1月にも高速列車同士が衝突し、46人が死亡した。今回の事故との関連性は低いとみられるが、サンチェス氏は「1年に2件もの高速列車事故は容認できない」として、原因究明と再発防止に全力を挙げる姿勢を強調した。

title: ネパール高峰で発見の2遺体は邦人
body: 【ニューデリー共同】在ネパール日本大使館は29日、ネパール中部のガンガプルナ西峰（標高7140メートル）で23日に見つかった2人の遺体がいずれも日本人だと確認したと明らかにした。登頂を目指していたが15日から連絡が取れなくなっていた。現地警察が死亡した状況を調べている。警察や関係者によると、2人はいずれも本籍が東京都の種石英典さん（40）と橋本哲さん（25）。標高4900メートル地点までネパール人の山岳ガイドが案内したが、その後は2人で登り、7050メートル地点まで到達したとの15日の連絡を最後に行方が分からなくなった。

title: 習近平総書記 4期目入りが濃厚
body:
【北京＝東慶一郎】北京で開催されていた中国共産党の重要会議・第２０期中央委員会第５回総会（５中総会）が２９日、閉幕した。国営新華社通信が伝えた声明には、習近平（シージンピン）総書記（国家主席）の後継含みとなる人事はなく、来年の党大会での習氏の４期目入りが濃厚となった。【写真】高市首相、ＶＩＶＡＮＴは「年末年始にまとめ見できたら」
総会では、軍幹部の相次ぐ失脚で、習氏を含む２人だけとなっていた軍指導機関・中央軍事委員会のナンバー２である副主席に文民が選出されるかが焦点の一つだった。習氏と前任の胡錦濤（フージンタオ）氏が、総書記就任前の中央委員会総会で中央軍事委の副主席に選ばれた前例があったためだ。
だが今回、中央軍事委では、軍制服組の張昇民（ジャンションミン）副主席が中央委員（閣僚級）から党指導部の政治局員に昇格しただけで、補充人事はなかった。
新たな党指導部を決める第２１回党大会を来年後半に北京で開くことも決めた。この時期に後継者と見なされる人物が浮上しないことは、習氏が事実上、次期党大会以降も軍と党を掌握し続けることが既定路線になったと言える。
昨年９月に突然交代が発表された劉建超（リウジエンチャオ）・前中央対外連絡部長ら党幹部３３人に対する党籍剥奪（はくだつ）処分も正式決定した。

title: 中国共産党 幹部ら33人の党籍剝奪
body: 北京で開かれていた中国共産党中央委員会第5回全体会議（5中全会）が29日、閉幕した。発表されたコミュニケ（公表文）によると、党指導部による汚職摘発などの実績を誇示し、問題を起こして役職を外れた党幹部らの大量処分も明らかにした。来年秋の党大会に向け、習近平（シーチンピン）総書記（国家主席）の権力基盤をさらに強固にした形だ。【写真】「指導部への登竜門」はいま　「ポスト習」はどこにコミュニケでは、習氏を核心とする党中央が「長年取り除けなかった根深い弊害を正し、党、国家、軍内部に潜んでいた重大な危険を取り除いた」と成果を誇った。一方、党内統治は「多くの新たな状況と問題に直面している」と指摘。そのうえで、6月に打ち出された「習近平党建設思想」について、毛沢東思想や鄧小平理論などと並んで党が貫くべきものと強調し、習氏を核心として一致結束するよう呼びかけた。各部門トップらへの監督や、汚職防止のための法制度を強化することも打ち出した。全体会議では、すでに党籍剝奪（はくだつ）が公表されていた軍制服組トップの張又俠・前中央軍事委員会副主席ら33人の処分が正式決定したほか、1人が党内職務を解かれた。党籍剝奪となった33人の中には、一時は次期外相の有力候補ともみられていた劉建超・前中央対外連絡部長も含まれていた。日本の政治家との交流も深かったが、昨年7月を最後に消息が途絶え、失脚の可能性が取りざたされていた。一方、昨年の4中全会で中央軍事委副主席に昇進した張昇民氏は、政治局員への昇格が決まった。その下のランクである中央委員は24人が処分された一方、補充は10人にとどまっており、腐敗からの党の立て直しは道半ばだ。コミュニケでは、2027年後半に北京で次期党大会を開催することも発表された。習氏の後継候補は今回の会議に伴う人事でも見当たらず、習氏が続投するとの見方がさらに強まりそうだ。（北京=平賀拓哉、小早川遥平）

title: ANA AIRDOなど完全子会社化へ
body:
ＡＮＡホールディングス（ＨＤ）は２９日、中堅航空会社「ＡＩＲＤＯ（エア・ドゥ）」と「ソラシドエア」を傘下に持つ「リージョナルプラスウイングス（ＲＰＷ）」を完全子会社化すると正式発表した。ＡＮＡＨＤの規模を生かした機材の一括調達や空港施設の機能集約などを進め、経営環境が厳しい国内線の収益改善を狙う。【写真】北九州を拠点にするライバルは「漆黒の翼」と親しまれている
ＡＮＡＨＤは現在、ＲＰＷ株を約１５％保有する。株式交換で、ＲＰＷ株を約２６％保有する日本政策投資銀行などから株式を取得する予定だ。２０２７年４月の子会社化完了を目指す。
エア・ドゥ、ソラシドのブランドは当面維持するが、将来的にはＡＮＡブランドへの統合も視野に入れる。現時点で人員削減や地方路線を廃止・減便する予定はないとしている。
エア・ドゥは北海道を、ソラシドエアは九州・沖縄を拠点に羽田などに就航している。両社は新型コロナ禍による収益悪化を受け、２２年に共同持ち株会社のＲＰＷを設立し、カウンター業務など一部業務の統合を進めてきた。
現在エア・ドゥが１２機、ソラシドエアが１４機の機材を保有している。国内線は円安などによる燃料高の影響を受けて収益性が低下しており、運航計画を一体的に定めることで、国内線の収益性向上や路線の維持をはかる。
各社の国内線事業は、コロナ後の需要減や燃料費や人件費の上昇などで収支が悪化している。国土交通省のまとめでは、国内主要６社の２５年３月期の決算は、公的支援を除けば本業のもうけを示す営業損益が赤字になった。国交省の有識者会議は今年５月、国内線の構造改革に向け、航空会社間での運航ダイヤの調整、大手から中堅への出資に関するルールを見直し、協業も可能としていた。

title: 欧州中銀 2会合ぶり金利据え置き
body: 【ロンドン時事】欧州中央銀行（ECB）は29日、ユーロ圏の金融政策を協議する定例理事会を開き、政策金利を2会合ぶりに据え置くことを決めた。主要政策金利の一つで、民間銀行がECBに資金を預ける際に適用する中銀預入金利を2．5％のまま維持する。中東での紛争に伴いエネルギー価格の高騰が続いているものの、今年に入り既に2回実施した利上げの経済への影響を慎重に見極める。ECBは声明で「エネルギーショックの完全な影響はまだ表れていないが、現時点では基調的なインフレは安定しており、賃金に目立った動きは見られない」と分析。ただ「（エネルギーショックの）規模が大きく、長引いていることから、今後はインフレ率を押し上げ、経済成長を低下させる可能性が高い」と指摘した。

title: 中部電 27年3月期の特損3800億円
body: 中部電力は29日、2027年3月期連結決算で浜岡原発（静岡県御前崎市）に関する特別損失として3800億円程度を計上すると発表した。【ひと目でわかる】中部電力浜岡原発データ不正の構図これにより純損益は2150億円の赤字（従来予想は1600億円の黒字）に転落し、過去最大の赤字となる見込み。同社は9月、浜岡原発のデータ不正問題を受け、再稼働に向けた審査の申請を取り下げた。その結果、将来の事業の見通しが不透明になったことから関連資産の減損損失を計上した。安全対策工事の費用増加も想定されるという。ただ、安井稔社長は記者会見で「今回の減損損失は浜岡原発の廃止を意味するものではない」と強調した。同時発表した26年9月中間連結決算でも浜岡関連の特損を計上し、純損益は2804億円の赤字（前年同期は1663億円の黒字）となった。

title: 11月電気代 大手7社で過去最高値
body: 中東情勢の悪化による資源価格の高騰を受け、11月使用分の電気料金は、大手電力10社のうち、7社で過去最高値を更新しました。【画像で見る】“住宅ローン50年時代”に…若者に広がる背景とリアル大手電力10社は29日、11月使用分の電気料金を発表しました。東京電力管内の平均的な家庭の場合、11月使用分の電気料金は前の月と比べて177円高くなり、9738円になります。東京電力のほか、東北電力や中部電力など7社で電気料金は過去最高値を更新しました。また、日本ガス協会は11月使用分のガス料金について、大手都市ガス4社すべてで値上がりすると発表しました。東京ガス管内では、前の月と比べて230円高くなり、6718円となります。中東情勢が再び悪化するなか、石油やLNG＝液化天然ガスなどの資源価格が高騰していて、電気・ガス料金は今後も値上がりする可能性があります。これを受け、政府は冬の電気・ガス代を補助する方向で検討を進めています。

title: のぞみ1hで14本運行目指す JR
body: JR東海は、東海道新幹線「のぞみ」のピーク時の運行本数を増やす方針を明らかにしました。JR東海によりますと、「のぞみ」は現在、ピーク時に最大で1時間あたり13本運行されていますが、大型連休などの繁忙期には指定席が満席になる時間帯が発生しています。そのため来年3月に行われる予定のダイヤ改正で、「のぞみ」を1時間あたり13本運行できる時間帯を拡大したうえで、将来的には1時間あたり14本運行するダイヤの実現を目指すとしています。具体的な導入時期は未定だということです。

title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
summary: The PM's Likud party has alleged foreign interference and said Arab-led parties "stole" the election after his coalition lost its majority.
body:
Activists with a placard saying "Love your neighbour" urge opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government that includes Arab-led parties
The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Arab-led parties including the Joint List headed by Yousef Jabareen (C) won a record 19 seats and could play a kingmaker role
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Netanyahu shares AI image on day of Israeli election
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

title: Audio reveals exchanges between Spain train operators and drivers moments before deadly crash
summary: The leaked tapes appear to show one high-speed train was given clearance to move at normal speed, even though another up ahead had stalled.
body:
Listen: Audio recordings between train driver and controller
Leaked audio recordings that were published in Spanish media have revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before a deadly crash on Wednesday morning, that has killed 69 people.
Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train near Urda.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".
Dozens of people were injured, with survivors recounting harrowing scenes people crying and bleeding, passengers trapped in their seats, missing limbs and smoke billowing throughout the carriages, one of which caught fire.
On Thursday, Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited some of the injured passengers in a hospital in Toledo.
He later expressed condolences to the victims' relatives, pledging that the investigation would determine why the crash happened, and what measures would be taken for this not to happen again.
Young athlete and former minister among victims of Spain train crash
The crash is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. On Thursday, the country began three days of national mourning.
The moving train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. The stationary train was run by private operator Iryo, and carrying 147 passengers.
A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Spain's transport minister.
The audio recordings were published by several Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE.
In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties.
After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."
The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."
The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.
The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.
The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.
Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente said on Wednesday that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
Watch: 'Chaotic scenes' at site of Spain's deadly train crash
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X  that they were "despicable".
Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
From the crash site, Sánchez said: "We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again."
Most Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements and suspended their campaigning ahead of a snap election on 29 November.
The exception is the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Protesters gathered outside the transport ministry offices in Madrid on Wednesday night
Overnight, around 1,500 people gathered outside the Spanish transport ministry building in the capital, according to broadcaster TVE, which reported that demonstrators were largely calling for the resignations of Sánchez and Puente.
Police used tear gas to disperse crowds after protesters hurled bottles and flares. No injuries or arrests were reported.
Rail drivers went ahead with a planned strike on Thursday, with the Spanish Union of Railway Drivers (Semaf) saying the strike action was being held "in defence of railway safety".
The leader of Spain's main opposition People's Party Alberto Núñez Feijóo said: "Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure."
At the crash site, emergency crews worked through the night under powerful floodlights to cut open metal carriages in the search for victims, with many of those killed in the crash still to be identified.
Hundreds of personnel have been deployed to the disaster site to assist with recovery efforts, Spain's interior ministry said, with drones and helicopters being used to find victims and remove rubble.
A spokesperson for the Spanish Civil Guard told the BBC they had deployed more than 900 people from different specialist departments, and the priority now was identifying the deceased.
They said they did not know how long this would take, but urged those with missing family members to go to one of the local centres which have been set up to offer DNA samples.

title: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
summary: A temporary ceasefire has brought rare quiet to Kherson, offering its residents a glimpse of normal life before fighting resumes.
body:
The temporary ceasefire in Kherson has provided its residents with the first glimpse of peace in nearly five years
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
"We've managed to adapt to this way of life," Olga said. "We've been living under these conditions for nearly five years now."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns.Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years agoby a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

title: Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
summary: At least 14 others were wounded in the attack in the central city of Dnipro, including an 11-year-old boy.
body:
The site of the drone strike has been sealed off, as Ukrainian authorities continue their investigation
At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to the railway operator chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform" when the drone struck, he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit an electric civilian train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole in a platform that is strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7sanctions on Russiaand repeated his criticism of a controversial deal that was struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Moscow, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 25 others, including four children, were injured, he added.
A day of mourning has been declared for Chernihiv and Dnipro on Friday.
In the city of Kremenchuk, in the central Poltava region, three people were killed and 28 injured in a Russian drone attack that hit residential buildings and a school, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said.
At least 25 people were injured in the Russian strike on Kremenchuk, local officials said
The latest Russian strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residentshave been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricityfor years.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The two-day event is attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real, and attacks on Ukraine's train infrastructure have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency.
Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks,with two bridges attacked in the capital Kyiv, and a metro train hitduring one of the strikes.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself 'leader of Brazil' after election loss
summary: The defeated presidential candidate says he will lead the opposition from the US.
body:
Flávio Bolsonaro arrived in Florida on Wednesday
The defeated candidate in Brazil's presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro, has referred to himself as "leader of Brazil" in a letter he published on social media after leaving the country for the United States.
Bolsonaro lost to his left-wing rival, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the run-off on Sunday by a difference of 4.4 million votes, but has not conceded defeat.
In the letter, Bolsonaro alleges, without offering evidence, that he was the victim of "electoral fraud" and says that he will lead the opposition from the US.
He left Brazil on Tuesday after failing to comply with an order to surrender his passports, a decision which Lula described as "a shameful act".
Watch: Has Flávio Bolsonaro left Brazil to evade justice?
Bolsonaro starts his letter, which he posted on his X account, saying "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the leader of Brazil".
However, he had posted a previous version, that was later deleted, in which he wrote: "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the rightful president of Brazil."
Both versions repeat the allegation that Bolsonaro first made on election night, that an extension of polling hours on Sunday had benefited his rival.
In the letter, he says it was "an electoral fraud unfolding before my eyes".
The extension was requested by both Lula's and Bolsonaro's campaign teams, and the head of Brazil's electoral authority has said that the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.
An analysis of election data conducted by BBC Brazil and BBC Verifyhas also found that only around 34,000 people voted during the extended hours - far lower than the 4.4 million votes that separated Lula from Bolsonaro.
In his letter, Bolsonaro also addresses his departure from Brazil -which caused confusion after he disappeared for more than 24 hours.
It later emerged that he had gone across the land border to Argentina, and from there flew on to Florida, following a brief refuelling stop in Ecuador.
Bolsonaro left after failing to hand in his passports to police - in defiance of a Supreme Court order, which had been issued as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering.
He has not been charged as part of the money laundering probe and denies any wrongdoing, calling the investigation a "politically-motivated witch hunt".
Bolsonaro added that he had never intended to leave Brazil, but argued that he was the victim of "political persecution".
He ended the letter by saying: "I left Brazil but I haven't abandoned Brazilians".
While Flávio Bolsonaro said that he planned to lead the opposition from the US, it was not clear how he planned to do that.
His party recognised the election result and while some of its politicians have described Bolsonaro as a "political exile", his campaign manager, Rogério Marinho, stated on Wednesday that "there is no evidence" of the electoral fraud that Bolsonaro alleges took place.
It is also not yet clear where Bolsonaro intends to stay or for how long.
His younger brother, Eduardo, has been inself-imposed exile in the US since March 2025, saying he was the victim of political persecution. The two siblings posted a photo of themselves holding a Brazilian flag on Wednesday.
Flávio Bolsonaro's brother Eduardo posted a photo of the two of them in the US
The Trump administration has provided visas for Flávio Bolsonaro and his family but did not say what kind of visas they were.
The US president did not explicitly endorse Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election and told reporters he "won't get involved" when asked about Bolsonaro's allegations of election fraud.
Earlier in the week, he had said that "it looked like another rigged election," without providing any evidence.
And on Thursday, Trump told reporters that "the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil".

title: Crypto worth billions frozen after suspected Binance hack
summary: The firm said transactions are suspended while it conducts security checks and will "cover all losses".
body:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that it has frozen digital assets worth around $3bn (£2.24bn) to prevent them from being stolen while it investigates a security issue.
The company said as part of a series of alerts online that all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while its teams conduct security checks and that the firm will "cover all losses".
"It does look like a hack on Binance," said Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao, who remains a majority shareholder of the firm.
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they have also frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.
Binance said the amount of funds frozen may continue to increase as its teams work closely with law enforcement and other partners to trace and seize additional assets.
"We are working around the clock and will share a full post-mortem once the investigation is complete. Please rely only on official Binance channels for updates," the firm said, adding that users' funds are safe.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.
Bitcoin dropped by around 5% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.
Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said his firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident.
Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen around $1.6bn "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."
"Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," said Ardoino, whose company issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT.
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the attack.
The scale of the attack is still unclear.
In 2025,hackers stole $1.5bn in cryptofrom the Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange Bybit. The record-breaking incident has been attributed to hackers linked with North Korea.

title: Google value plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
summary: Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its AI search summaries were affecting ad revenue.
body:
Google CEO Sundar Pichai has backed the company's massive spending on AI.
Google parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations.
Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue.
Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.
Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.
However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And forthe second time in its historyas a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.
Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.
By the end of Thursday,  the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter.
The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.
Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Wall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this weekplans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
summary: Poundland's bosses are filing a notice of intention to appoint administrators to the business.
body:
Andy Burnham has said the government is "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.
The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, was rejected.
"This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC.
The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).
Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case.
"We stand ready to support the workforce however we can."
The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.
The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told its 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.
It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.
Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, which has left it on the brink of collapse.
It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off.
Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, and has around 20 million customers per year.
It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.
It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.
The curious case of why Poundland is struggling during a cost-of-living crisis
Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer
A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allowcreditors to recover more money, and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff.The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.
If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.
These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interestedin takingon between 200 and 250 stores.
Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.
More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.
Bally Auluk, a national officer at the Usdaw shopworkers union, said this week had been "incredibly distressing" for Poundland staff.
He claimed staff were having to "watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1".

title: US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you
summary: The Federal Reserve's interest rate decisions affect everything from mortgages to car loans
body:
The US Federal Reserve has held interest rates steady at 3.75% - 4%.
The decision comes within a week of the midterm elections and after the central bank raised interest rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting.
"The overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgement, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said, referring to September's interest rate rise.
Figures published after the Fed's announcement showed the US economy growing at a stronger pace than expected, with inflation running above the Fed's target.
An interest rate tells people and businesses how much it costs to borrow money – such as with credit cards, mortgages, or business loans – but also what return they get for saving cash.
The Fed influences interest rates in the US through its target range for the federal funds rate, which is the interest rate used by commercial banks for overnight borrowing.
In its decision to hold rates steady this month, the Fed said that while inflation remains high, it wanted to gather more information before making another decision to change rates.
The Fed also noted that while there was uncertainty, the US economy remained resilient.
Warsh acknowledged that inflation remained too high, but noted that there were other signs - such as tightening credit conditions - that the economy was moving in the right direction.
There is plenty more economic data to come between now and the committee's next meeting, the Fed chair added, which should paint a more detailed picture of the state of the economy.
At that point, Warsh said, "we'll be, I think, better positioned to determine the right policy decision and the stance of policy."
While last month the committee signalled there could be one more rate rise this year, Warsh would not be drawn out on where he thinks they will go in six weeks' time.
"A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings."
The decision to hold rates steady was not unanimous.
While 10 of the 12 committee members voted to keep rates unchanged, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted to increase rates to 4%-4.25%, from its current 3.75%-4%.
The bank's next meeting will be held over 8-9 December.
Warsh said things are moving in the right direction, while the US economy is performing very strongly.
The US economy grew by 3.4% on an annualised basis in the three months to September, stronger than analysts had expected.
That strong growth was driven by an acceleration in investment, and strong consumer spending.
While there was an annualised increase in personal spending of 3.8%, the annualised increase in private investment was a huge 19.4% which analysts say was largely due to investment in artificial intelligence.
Inflation is also above the Fed's target range.
Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices which have surged off the back of the war in Iran.
The Fed uses interest rate changes to try to keep inflation –the rate at which prices change– at 2% a year and keep the job market stable.
When inflation is too high, the Fed tends to raise interest rates.
This tends to mean higher rates from banks and other lenders, which in turn affects spending and saving decisions.
For example, someone refinancing their mortgage or buying a property for the first time could face higher mortgage rates. It could also mean higher interest rates on credit cards or car loans. However, it means higher interest rates on savings as well.
This encourages people and businesses to save more, spend less money, and make less investments. It also encourages companies to hire less people or slow the pace of pay rises.
All of this tends to reduce demand and slow inflation.
When inflation is low or if the Fed believes the economy needs a boost, it cut rates.
The idea is that this will have the opposite affect, with banks dropping rates leading to more spending and less saving from people and businesses.
Leaving the rates unchanged means rates on things like new mortgages or business loans are also less likely to change. It also means interest rates on cash savings are unlikely to rise.
US interest rates have historically moved around quite a bit.
The last time Fed rates were as high as they have been recently was in the lead up to and during the start of the 2008 global financial crisis.
The Fed then dropped rates to historic lows to encourage spending and job creation during the economic slump and kept them at those lows for several years.
They picked up again ahead of the pandemic before dropping to as low as 0%-0.25% during the pandemic. They then rose to highs of 5.25%-5% from the middle of 2023 to August 2024 as inflation jumped.
They had been falling steadily since then, until rates were raised last month.

title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
summary: Budget forecasts show growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.
body:
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.
Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.
"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.
However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains "already behind us".

The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.

title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
summary: Opponents have questioned the Budget's lack of detail on welfare reform, with the prime minister not outlining a timetable for any reductions.
body:
Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.
Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.
Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."
He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".
Budget 2026: Key points at a glance
The prime minister faced questions about his approach afterthe Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBCthat the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.
When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."
But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".
The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.
Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.
These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.
The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his  attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.
Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.
He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."
Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.
"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."
Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane said if the government could provide a plan to show "greater restraint" of the benefits bill, that would "play spectacularly well" with the financial markets.
Haldane, who has previously advised Burnham, told the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast: "If the government could get that through I think it would come with a huge bonus."
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".
Reacting to government briefings and remarks on Thursday related to when a reduction in the benefits bill could take place, Badenoch said it "looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading".
She said: "Don't let anyone tell you this was a 'do no harm budget'. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they've harmed our national security."
Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.
Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.
Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.
The government has already pledged toreform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030, and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.

title: DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
summary: The DUP leader Gavin Robinson also confirms that Emma Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill.
body:
Michelle O'Neill described the move as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented"
Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has been blocked by the DUP from attending an economic summit involving Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The Sinn Féin vice-president and Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly were both invited to attend the National Economic Council in Glasgow on Friday with other devolved leaders.
The DUP leader Gavin Robinson confirmed that his party colleague Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill and permission will not be granted for the first minister to operate on a solo basis.
The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order march in Portadownfrom passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
Robinson was flanked by DUP assembly members as he spoke in the Great Hall at Parliament Buildings
A meeting of the party's ruling officer committee was held earlier on Thursday.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the first minister's "arrogance will have consequences", but O'Neill accused the party of being "reckless and irresponsible".
"Her complaints today that she's frustrated from engaging with the British Prime Minister within the sovereign United Kingdom will so be it because her law breaking must have consequences," Robinson said.
O'Neill said the DUP leader's comments were "arrogant and supremacist" adding that the DUP "is consumed with their own internal leadership troubles and divisions".
She said she would be at the Assembly on Monday with her party colleagues to "keep showing up every day for people".
Earlier she described the move to block the meeting with the prime minister as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented".
"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems," she said in a statement posted online.
The prime minister revived the National Economic Council over the summer to encourage greater collaboration between the nations and regions.
Earlier Little-Pengelly said the concerns arising from O'Neill's conduct and the "anger and hurt felt by many people across Northern Ireland, cannot simply be ignored or minimised".
She said the decision comes after stopping a separate planned engagement with the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly.
"I have requested a separate meeting with the Prime Minister to ensure Northern Ireland's interests, including the urgent budgetary and funding challenges facing the Executive, continue to be represented directly," she added.
The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it was "deeply frustrating" that the Northern Ireland executive would not be represented at the National Economic Council.
"I understand feelings are running high but it must be in the interests of the people of Northern Ireland that everyone gets round the table."
The DUP ruling committee met to discuss what steps it would take against Sinn Féin over the Drumcree dispute
O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin figureshave been interviewed by police investigating last month's unnotified demonstrations in Portadown, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.
The Sinn Féin deputy leader has defended her involvement, saying it was the "right thing to do".
The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said "the DUP's sham response today was beyond pathetic" adding "the DUP is interested only in clinging to office, not principle".
Alliance leader Naomi Long said refusing to attend or preventing others from attending the meeting with the prime minister was reckless and put party interests ahead of Northern Ireland's economic future and the needs of the public.
The Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows told BBC's Evening Extra programme the situation was a "political fudge" that was "all choreography and no consequences," adding that the move would "probably galvanise Sinn Féin further at the ballot box."
The Social Democratic and Labour Party's (SDLP) Matthew O'Toole said "plunging this place into more political chaos is not a sensible strategic move for unionism".
"Ultimately it's only going to make reasonable people here conclude that the largest unionist party simply doesn't want to make the status quo work," he added.
The DUP has been under pressure from unionist rivals and some within its own ranks over how to respond to the row over Drumcree.
Last week,DUP MP Carla Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer boardover their leader Gavin Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.
On Thursday Lockhart said she will follow her "own course" if the party does not seek to remove Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill as Stormont's first minister.
Robinson said that while O'Neill and her party colleagues "should be punished, that does not include punishing the rest of Northern Ireland".
The Upper Bann MP, who last week quit the DUP's ruling officer board in opposition to party leader Gavin Robinson's approach, outlined her position in a letter to colleagues which she later posted on Facebook.
Other DUP representatives including assembly member Diane Forsythe have since backedLockhart's calls for O'Neill to be "removed from office".
On Tuesday, Forsythe said that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".
On Wednesday, a second DUP assembly member called for O'Neill to go.
Maurice Bradley said removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the Assembly to collapse".
Carla Lockhart stepped down from the DUP's officer board last week
Bradley added that the party "must stand together" and "support Carla Lockhart".
Other party members including former MP Lord McCrea and Mid Ulster councillor Clement Cuthbertson have also backed Lockhart.
Party leader Robinson said last week that he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".
Speaking on theBBC's The View programme, Robinson said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.
He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".
"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.
Last week, a court heard Police Service of Northern Ireland intelligence information thatdissidents may have mounted gun attackson police had officers cleared a path for the parade.

title: Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
summary: The Lib Dems claim Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accuses the party of "lying".
body:
Watch: Parliament's live broadcast showed the moments surrounding the alleged incident
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.
The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.
Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.
The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".
The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."
Footage, firstunearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.
However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in theclip originally posted by the Telegraph,external.
The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.
Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.
In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.
"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.
"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."
Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."
Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."
Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage
The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.
In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.
"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.
A spokesperson for the House of Commons said that a prayer card for Farage - the way in which MPs reserve seats in the Commons - did not "display a valid date stamp" and therefore "was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol".

title: Further delays for major council overhaul in nine of 14 proposed areas
summary: Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger unitary authorities were put on hold last month.
body:
Local government minister Jim McMahon has announced plans in five areas will go ahead
The government has announced further delays to nine of 14 major council mergers, with only five now going ahead.
Proposals for 14 regions to undergo mergers of smaller councils to form larger unitary authorities wasput on holdby Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner last month, following concerns around legal challenges.
Local Government Minister Jim McMahon has told MPs the review had found the government's decision-making to be "robust", but nine areas have now been withdrawn for further review.
Only five of the original 14 regions will be taken forward, after three more weeks of consultation. Shadow local government secretary Katie Lam condemned the latest news as "a farce".
Mergers will continue to progress in East Sussex, Gloucestershire,Oxfordshire, Warwickshire andWorcestershire.
But the government is seeking "legal clarity" in the remaining nine areas, which are:Derbyshire,Devon,Hertfordshire, Kent, Lancashire,Leicestershire,Lincolnshire,Nottinghamshire, and Staffordshire.
In a Commons statement, McMahon said the government was "withdrawing the decisions announced in July" for those nine areas.
"I want to be absolutely clear that this is not a reflection of the work underpinning those proposals," he added.
The review will now focus on the nine areas where current plans have been withdrawn for further review, as well as four areas where plans were withdrawn in September, inEssex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.
Two further areas, Cambridgeshire and West Sussex, are still waiting for merger plans to be agreed, totalling 15 regions where local government reorganisation plans remain undecided.
McMahon said: "We will move faster where we can, and some of the remaining areas may receive an outcome decision before others.
"I commit to coming back to the House with updates for another set of areas by Christmas, and every area will have an outcome by early next year."
Reconfirming local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries, he announced plans for elections to shadow councils, set to run for a year before taking over from old authorities, will now be held in May 2028.
Responding, Lam set out how the reorganisation had been beset by delays over the past two-and-a-half years.
"From start to finish this government's approach to local government reorganisation has been nothing short of a farce," she told MPs.
She added: "Naturally the taxpayer was left to pick up the tab for all of these delays - a bill which runs into the tens of millions of pounds."
Local Government Association chair Eamonn O'Brien called for a re-set of relations between the government and local councils across the country.
He said: "While today's announcement provides some certainty for some areas, many councils remain frustrated by the situation they have been placed in.
"All councils affected need urgent clarity on next steps and how costs already incurred will be met.
"There needs to be a reset in the relationship between government and councils on local government reorganisation, with local government fully engaged in shaping decisions from the outset."
